domain.title: Web and APIs
domain.summary: How clients and servers communicate over HTTP, and how to design APIs that behave predictably under real network conditions.

concepts.title: HTTP request lifecycle
concepts.summary: A request message (method, URL, headers, body) passes through server routing and middleware to handler code, and a response (status, headers, body, possibly streamed) travels back, with failure or client disconnection possible at every hop.
learningObjectives: Trace a request from a client call through middleware to a handler and back
Explain where headers, body, and status are set and read
Identify where latency and failures can occur along the path
recognitionSignals: middleware ordering, matchers, or route-registration order
reading request headers or setting response headers, redirects, or rewrites
streaming responses or handlers that observe client disconnect (e.g. request abort signals)
proxying or forwarding requests between services
misconceptionPatterns: Believing a request either fully succeeds or fully fails
Assuming middleware runs for every route regardless of registration order or matcher configuration
Believing server-side work automatically stops when the client disconnects

concepts.title: HTTP methods and status codes
concepts.summary: Methods declare intended semantics (safe, idempotent, or neither) that servers must actually honor; status codes tell clients and intermediaries what happened and whether retrying or caching makes sense.
learningObjectives: Distinguish safe, idempotent, and non-idempotent methods
Choose appropriate status codes for validation, auth, conflict, and server errors
Explain how status codes drive client retry and caching behavior
recognitionSignals: choice of HTTP method for a new endpoint, especially GET handlers that change state
explicit status codes set in responses or thrown HTTP errors
client code branching on response.status or response.ok
401 versus 403 versus 404 decisions
misconceptionPatterns: Believing a failure reported only in a 200 response body will be treated as a failure by clients, caches, retries, and monitoring
Believing 403 is the right response when credentials are missing or invalid, or 401 when an authenticated user lacks permission
Assuming fetch rejects on 4xx and 5xx responses
Believing a GET handler that changes state is harmless because only your own UI calls it

concepts.title: Serialization and JSON
concepts.summary: Turning in-memory values into bytes for transport or storage and back again, and what gets lost along the way.

related.boundary: Validating untrusted payloads against a schema maps there; what a wire format preserves or exposes maps here.

learningObjectives: Predict how dates, big integers, undefined, NaN, and Maps survive a JSON round-trip
Identify precision loss when 64-bit IDs or decimal amounts pass through JSON or floating-point numbers
Identify accidental over-exposure of fields in serialized responses and compare explicit response mapping with returning database objects directly
recognitionSignals: encoding or decoding data at a process boundary (JSON.stringify/parse, protobuf, form data)
DTO or response mapping functions that choose which fields are exposed
Date, decimal, or 64-bit numeric ID fields crossing an API
handlers returning whole ORM or database rows
misconceptionPatterns: Assuming large integer IDs or decimal money values survive JSON and floating-point numbers without precision loss
Believing Dates round-trip through JSON as Date objects
Believing fields the UI does not display are not exposed to users

concepts.title: REST resource design
concepts.summary: Modeling an API as resources with consistent URLs, methods, and representations so clients can reason about it.
learningObjectives: Evaluate whether routes model resources or leak implementation actions
Compare REST resources with RPC-style endpoints or framework RPC mechanisms (e.g. server actions, tRPC) for a given use case
Design error and versioning conventions an API can keep
recognitionSignals: URL paths that name actions (e.g. /createOrder, /getUsers)
nested resource URLs
API versioning prefixes or headers
shared error envelope types
renamed or removed fields in API response types
misconceptionPatterns: Believing a response field can be renamed or removed safely because the frontend was updated in the same deploy
Believing resource URLs should name actions (e.g. POST /deleteUser) rather than resources acted on by HTTP methods
Assuming each endpoint can use its own ad-hoc error shape without cost to clients

concepts.title: Authentication vs. authorization
concepts.summary: Authentication establishes who is making a request; authorization decides whether that identity may perform this action on this resource.

related.boundary: CSRF and SSRF map there; missing ownership or role checks map here.
Scopes of tokens, service roles, and integrations map there; per-request permission checks map here.

learningObjectives: Distinguish identity verification from permission checks in a handler
Identify endpoints that authenticate but never check ownership or role
Explain where authorization must be enforced server-side and why client checks are insufficient
recognitionSignals: current-user or session lookup used to gate a handler, page, or RPC endpoint
queries by resource ID that do or do not also filter by owner, user, or tenant
role, permission, or policy checks
access restricted only in UI components or client-side route guards
misconceptionPatterns: Believing a logged-in user may access any resource whose ID they know
Believing hiding a button or page in the UI prevents the underlying endpoint from being called
Believing an authentication check in middleware also enforces per-resource permissions in every handler

concepts.title: Pagination
concepts.summary: Returning large collections in bounded pages, using offsets or cursors, so responses stay fast and consistent.
learningObjectives: Compare offset and cursor pagination under concurrent inserts
Explain why unbounded list endpoints become availability risks
Design a stable sort order for cursor pagination
recognitionSignals: limit/offset or skip/take parameters
cursor, after, or nextPageToken fields
list endpoints or queries without a limit
ORDER BY on a non-unique column combined with LIMIT or a cursor
calls to paginated third-party APIs with or without a next-page loop
misconceptionPatterns: Assuming offset pagination never skips or duplicates rows
Believing a timestamp or other non-unique column alone gives a stable cursor order
Assuming a single call to a paginated API returns the complete result set
Letting clients request arbitrarily large page sizes

concepts.title: Retry strategies
concepts.summary: Re-attempting failed calls can mask transient faults, but only with limits, backoff, jitter, and awareness of what is safe to repeat.

related.boundary: What happens after attempts are exhausted (failed states, dead letters) maps there; attempt policy and backoff map here.

learningObjectives: Decide which failures are worth retrying and which are not
Explain exponential backoff and why jitter prevents synchronized retry storms
Identify retries that can duplicate side effects
recognitionSignals: retry loops or retry helper libraries
backoff, delay, or sleep between attempts
maxAttempts or retry count configuration
retries wrapped around POST or payment-like calls
misconceptionPatterns: Believing immediate, repeated retries help a struggling dependency recover
Treating every error as retryable, including 400 or 422 validation failures
Ignoring 429 responses and Retry-After hints when scheduling the next attempt
Assuming retries configured at several layers (client, SDK, server, queue) add up rather than multiply

concepts.title: Idempotency
concepts.summary: An idempotent operation has the same effect whether it runs once or many times, which is what makes retries safe.
learningObjectives: Predict the outcome when two requests with the same idempotency key arrive concurrently or after a crash mid-processing
Design an idempotency-key scheme with an atomic uniqueness guard and a stored result for replays
Evaluate which operations in a workflow are naturally idempotent and which need protection
recognitionSignals: Idempotency-Key headers or client-supplied request IDs
inserts or upserts keyed on a request, event, or delivery ID (e.g. ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING)
webhook or job handlers that may be delivered more than once
double-submit protection on forms or payment actions
misconceptionPatterns: Believing POST requests cannot be made idempotent
Believing it is safe to record an idempotency key only after the side effect succeeds
Believing a handler whose state update is idempotent (e.g. set status = 'paid') is safe to repeat even though it also triggers emails, charges, or other side effects

concepts.title: Same-origin policy and CORS
concepts.summary: Browsers stop scripts on one origin from reading responses from another unless the server opts in with CORS headers; CORS controls what browsers may read, not who can call the server.

related.boundary: Whether a cross-site request is honored (CSRF) maps there; whether its response can be read maps here.

learningObjectives: Predict whether a cross-origin browser request is sent directly, preflighted, or sent but blocked from being read
Explain why CORS does not stop non-browser clients or protect an endpoint from being called
Identify unsafe CORS configurations such as reflecting any Origin while allowing credentials
recognitionSignals: Access-Control-Allow-Origin, Access-Control-Allow-Credentials, or Access-Control-Allow-Headers response headers
CORS middleware or framework CORS configuration
OPTIONS preflight handlers
browser requests to another origin with credentials: 'include'
misconceptionPatterns: Believing CORS is a server-side access control that blocks unauthorized callers
Believing reflecting the request Origin with credentials allowed is a safe fix for a CORS error
Assuming a request whose response was blocked by CORS never reached or changed anything on the server
